newsitem.title: CHINA: U.S. told to stay out of China-Japan islands row.
newsitem.headline: U.S. told to stay out of China-Japan islands row.

text.p: China warned the United States on Tuesday not to intervene in dispute between Beijing and Tokyo over a group of islands in East China Sea.
"This is an issue between China and Japan and no third party may intervene in this matter," Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang told a briefing.
Shen had been asked to comment on a U.S. congressional report that had urged Washington to defend the islands based on a security pact signed by Washington and Tokyo last April.
"The U.S.-Japan security pact is a bilateral defence arrangement and cannot exceed this scope," Shen said.

"If it exceeds this bilateral scope or is targeted at the interests of a third party, it will certainly cause uneasiness and vigilance among neighbouring Asian countries, including China, and bring complicated factors into regional security," he said.

The U.S.-Japan security agreement pledged increased bilateral cooperation on intelligence, military technology transfers and other matters such as supply of ammunition and other material in peacetime.
Shen reiterated that the islands, claimed by Beijing and Taipei as the Diaoyus and by Tokyo as the Senkakus, were an inseparable part of China.
China has claimed sovereignty over the islands for centuries.
Tokyo's claim dates back to 1895, when it defeated imperial China and seized the islands. Japan says the issue is not open for discussion.

In 1972, Japan was given control of the islands by the United States, which had administered them along with Okinawa since the end of World War Two in 1945. But the U.S. government at the time said any outstanding territorial issue should be settled among the countries concerned.
Shen said China had declared then that the U.S. move to give Japan control of the islands was illegal.
"This was totally illegal. This could not change in the slightest the territorial sovereignty of the People's Republic of China over the Diaoyus," Shen said.
"This stand of the Chinese side is consistent, clear and unshakeable," he said.

Japan's claim to the uninhabited islands has triggered anti-Japanese demonstrations in Hong Kong and Taiwan since a Japanese right-wing group built a makeshift lighthouse on one of the islands in July.
Emotions were fanned last month when a Hong Kong activist drowned after he jumped into stormy waters around the island to demonstrate Chinese claims.

Last week, about 300 Taiwanese and Hong Kong protesters aboard a 50-boat flotilla pierced a Japanese maritime cordon around the islands and briefly raised the flags of Beijing and Taipei on the rocky outcrops in a challenge to Tokyo's claim of sovereignty.
Taipei has no diplomatic ties with Tokyo, which only recognises Beijing's Communist government.
Japan has sought to calm passions in the dispute and asked Taiwan to prevent a recurrence of the landings.
